title: Monopoly Round-Up: Wall Street Mocks Bernie Sanders as “Almost Dead”
author: Lee Hepner
content:
The big news of the week was obviously the midterm elections. Antimonopolists
soared in the midterms, as we [wrote
up](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/ten-things-to-know-about-this-crushing)
earlier in the week. There were lots of other things, too, like the CEO of the
most important chipmaker in the world being outed as having an affair with a
Chinese spy, a major media distribution merger that represents the further
consolidation of Hollywood and media, and one of the largest self-inflicted
breakups in history. We'll get into all of that. There's a lot of good and bad
news in the antimonopoly world, as usual, for paid subscribers after the jump.

First, I want to focus on the stock market crash last week, a decline that
took place because of the midterm elections. What's interesting is that the
attitude of Wall Street and Silicon Valley leaders is generally unchastened.
Many of those leaders lashed out publicly, making statements to the effect
that the actions of voters are irrelevant.

And yet, the financial carnage was real.

On Thursday, the markets took their biggest single-day dive in 18 months. The
S&P declined 4.36% and the NASDAQ ended the day down 5.52%, mostly centered in
chip and big tech stocks. Some $3 trillion in market capitalization on the S&P
500 was wiped out in a single day, in large part due to fear that the
Democratic wave election means the AI trade is over.

But here's Jason Calacanis, a tech investor, advisor to Elon Musk, and co-host
of the _All-In_ podcast, taking it all in stride and impugning the conviction
of voters:

Calacanis was expressing a common view among investors that elections don't
really matter. For instance, take 83-year old billionaire investor and Elon
Musk-ally Ron Baron, who
[appeared](https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/06/watch-cnbcs-full-interview-
with-baron-capital-founder-and-ceo-ron-baron.html) on CNBC just two days after
the election to give a preview of post-midterm investor mentality heading into
his annual [Baron Investment
Conference](https://www.baroncapitalgroup.com/conference-2026) (a name that
sounds fake but isn't). When asked whether he's concerned about Congressional
oversight hearings, targeting Musk or anyone else, he brushed it off. In fact,
asked about Bernie Sanders and his opposition to data centers, Baron exclaimed
"Who cares about him? He's almost dead."

That's a shift. In 2016, Baron went on a [press
tour](https://www.cnbc.com/2016/11/04/without-naming-names-billionaire-ron-
baron-says-one-candidate-would-hurt-the-economy.html) to talk about how much
sleep he'd been losing over the possibility of a Trump presidency. "For weeks
now, I've been so upset with this election. I wake up every night two or three
times," he said at the time. Now, however, when asked what he thinks about
potential turbulence for AI, he responds that he doesn't think about it. When
asked what he thought about the midterm elections, he said he "slept through
it," and added, "I don't think about elections."

Musk himself, who played the biggest role over the last few years in
conservative politics, aside from Trump himself, had a similar view. Texas,
his home state where he has also domiciled his companies, went to his avowed
political opponents. And yet, he simply dismissed any impact of the election
on his own choices.

These men are not anomalies. Two days after the election, as the AI industry
was facing the biggest market correction in well over a year, OpenAI CFO Sarah
Friars [said](https://archive.is/5DMs2#selection-2049.108-2049.177), "I don't
think there was something that dramatically changed for us." Their plan
following the midterms? Continue attracting capital investment, maintain Q3
momentum, keep course for an IPO, and -- wait for it -- rebrand "data centers"
as "compute campuses." Meta's President is saying something similar.

Or look at Google, which has been found liable by at least three federal
courts for illegally monopolizing markets spanning online search, digital
advertising, and app distribution. How did Google respond to the midterms?
They didn't even wait for the results.

On Election Day, Google
[announced](https://archive.is/53wB7#selection-8463.0-8471.260) it would turn
off classroom access to Google Search if schools sought to turn off Google's
AI tools. The backdrop here is the protracted and heated debate over the
impact of AI on learning outcomes and child psychology. In September, school
districts in both New York City and Los Angeles decided to restrict student
access to AI in the classroom. Google's response, to turn off its products
altogether, could be a form of illegal tying in violation of the same
antitrust law it has repeatedly violated.

There's a reason for this refusal to temper behavior in response to a
rejection by voters. Since the 1970s, no matter who is in office, big business
has done well. JP Morgan for example
[advises](https://www.jpmorgan.com/insights/markets-and-economy/markets/a-new-
presidential-race-is-on-know-the-potential-investment-implications) investors,
election after election, not to read too much into politics or election
results. Here's JP Morgan's Head of Investment Strategy Elyse Ausenbaugh in
2024:

> "Even as the politicians go and campaign on certain policy platforms, we
> should be very careful as investors about over-indexing any assumption how
> that may play out in markets."

And it's true. Seasoned investors have traditionally not cared about
elections. Republicans
[feel](https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2018/03/22/positive-views-of-
economy-surge-driven-by-major-shifts-among-republicans/) better about the
economy under Republican administrations, and Democrats feel better about the
economy under Democrat administrations, but whether it's Reagan or Clinton,
Obama or Trump, the [Number Go Up
Rule](https://www.thebignewsletter.com/p/the-number-go-up-rule-why-america)
has
[prevailed](https://assets.ctfassets.net/tpwhn4idgh34/1vM9UfetoeqZzQoRRGoTAk/b32bf6d5112df401190d7355f8a56721/RBA_Insights_Fade_the_election_9.24.pdf):

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3uDY!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F12c7d79e-a9e7-4555-8013-073dd360447e_961x549.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3uDY!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F12c7d79e-a9e7-4555-8013-073dd360447e_961x549.png)_The
economic context matters more than party control. The low overall performance
of Bush 43 reflects both 9/11 and the onset of the Global Financial Crisis._

In terms of precedent, markets tend to
[perform](https://www.cambridgeassociates.com/insight/planning-for-the-us-
presidential-election/a) well in the year following an election, at least over
the past half century:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TADm!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc39804aa-d8ea-45c0-a6f4-d43711c4cfb8_1010x629.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!TADm!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc39804aa-d8ea-45c0-a6f4-d43711c4cfb8_1010x629.png)_The
particularly high returns in the Democrat/Split column coincide with sharp
market recovery following the Global Financial Crisis._

But here's the thing. Economic populism hasn't been the basis for an election
this overwhelming since the 1930s. So all of those theories and precedents
from Wall Street are just guesses based on a questionable sample size.

Moreover, market indifference to politics is a bipartisan creation _of_
politics. For a recent example of this, rewind to the worst single-day in the
market prior to last week, which was April 4, 2025, two days after Trump
announced his Liberation Day tariffs. On that date 18 months ago, the S&P fell
5.97% and the NASDAQ fell 5.82% in a single day -- _worse_ than the midterm
wipeout. How did Trump respond to the market revolt? It took five days of
market turmoil for Trump to announce a 90-day pause to his reciprocal tariffs
rollout.

Trump's Liberation Day tariffs also faced the predictable partisan blowback,
and they attracted legitimate criticism because they were chaotic, punitive,
and non-strategic. But his capitulation was a response to the headwinds of
market turmoil, which reveals the boundaries of government's ability to manage
the economy.

Perhaps it's not surprising, then, to see investment kingpins bucking the
midterm election results.

### **Industry Unchastened?**

While _politics_ might not really matter to market outcomes, the threat of
actual _policymaking_ does. And here's where the stock market decline might
suggest something different than what the confidence of Musk, Baron, Frier,
and others implies.

Among the midterm mandates was a nearly universal, bipartisan rejection of
data centers. Dozens of local jurisdictions voted
[against](https://www.bizjournals.com/sanjose/news/2026/11/04/ai-data-center-
ballot-election-development-oppose.html) the construction of new data centers,
an illustration of their bipartisan unpopularity. Texas has been a major
target for data center construction and the climate now looks
[tougher](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/04/1148043/texas-was-the-
new-epicenter-of-the-ai-data-center-buildout-that-might-be-kaput/) there. And
then there are [predictions](https://heraldsphere.com/article/td-cowen-cuts-
odds-of-energy-permitting-bill-passing-to-25/) that Congress may not pass the
pending permitting reform bill. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs
Act, or "BAAJA," would be mostly good news for data center construction, if
only because it
[offers](https://www.energypolicy.columbia.edu/publications/what-the-
bipartisan-american-affordability-and-jobs-act-means-for-the-u-s-energy-
system/) the certainty that industry so craves to finance the build out.

Similarly, Google's moves are being met by anger from some of the most popular
and newer Democrats. Here's how Mayor Zohran Mamdani responded on X:

And here's what former FTC Chair and current Chair of NYC's Economic
Development Corporation Lina Khan had to
[say](https://archive.is/53wB7#selection-8471.0-8471.260):

> "This latest move shows it remains unchastened," Ms. Khan said of Google's
> new A.I. changes for schools. "As the public increasingly pushes back
> against the use of AI in schools," she added, "Google is making clear it
> will punish those who don't fall in line."

"Unchastened." And why wouldn't they be? Google has been found liable for
monopolization three times, and three times the remedy has done little. Why
would OpenAI be chastened by a politics that treats big business as above the
law? Why would Ron Baron be chastened by calls for accountability or controls
on SpaceX, whether coming from Bernie or the new crop of economic populists,
such that he would avoid going all in with Elon Musk on a merger of Tesla and
SpaceX?

But then, there is the matter of a market crash on Thursday. And ironically,
it was Donald Trump who acknowledged most notably that the election _did_
matter. Here's Trump on Truth Social blaming the tumbling market on "the
Dumocrats" and the voters themselves:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zlHQ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F698041bb-61e5-404e-a540-4f59570b2f3c_1078x663.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!zlHQ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F698041bb-61e5-404e-a540-4f59570b2f3c_1078x663.png)

Trump's major policy choice has been to inflate an AI bubble, or to invest in
U.S. dominance in AI, however you want to frame it. So the unwind over the
last few days could be seen as a test of whether that policy will remain in
place. With the dozens of ballot initiatives rejecting data centers, it's hard
to imagine there won't be a shift. Already, the initial public offering of
Anthropic, which is existential for Wall Street and Silicon Valley, is
[tottering](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-06/anthropic-ipo-
valuation-expectations-pressured-after-ai-rout).

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!6r3l!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4a6267c7-5575-4345-8e55-b531f2f5dd6a_1604x428.png)

Another signal is that previously untouchable figures, like Nvidia's CEO
Jensen Huang, are being exposed by enemies over scandals that were likely
known but kept under wraps.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c570!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc0659038-45f8-496f-96cf-d1270f47235c_1362x626.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!c570!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-
post-
media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fc0659038-45f8-496f-96cf-d1270f47235c_1362x626.png)

And some billionaires, like Calacanis' _All-In_ co-host Chamath Palihapitiya,
are now going on [apology
tours](https://x.com/LeeHepner/status/2119498078155932068?a=UtEdN9AeOcMrHiRTKOk&s=20)
to curry favor with the incoming Democrats, largely because they want to
remain relevant by maintaining access to power. Still, that's a shift.

So the question presented by the midterms and the market correction two days
later is whether businesses and investors will take voter anger seriously.
Does the "midterm mandate" herald the generational shift in our politics that
many are pointing to? Or will speculative industries continue to conduct
[moral
hazard](https://www.richmondfed.org/publications/research/econ_focus/2023/q1_federal_reserve),
with the safe assurance that if all goes awry, a bailout will come their way?

I don't know the answer to those questions. None of us do. I am burned by the
political betrayals of the last few decades, as are we all. I get why Wall
Street expects nothing to change. But I'm also chronically optimistic, and
just as it's arrogant to imagine that Wall Street has been defeated, it is
just as arrogant to dismiss the power of voters demanding something different.

Now, on to the full round-up of news. There are some incredible stories -
Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang was caught having an affair with a Chinese spy, and
that may deflate the AI bubble since Nvidia is at the center of the financing.
Anthropic's IPO is on the rocks, another existential moment. Plus Elizabeth
Warren is likely to be Chair of the Banking Committee and has private equity
on her mind. Oh, and CVS is preemptively breaking itself up to avoid
regulatory scrutiny. All of that and more below the jump, for paid subscribers
only.

If you haven't yet joined as a paying subscriber, I'll just note that this
newsletter has had a big impact on policy. We helped coin the term "Break Up
Big Medicine," we've helped launch dozens of antitrust suits against fire
truck makers, and we'll be doing a lot of work in this new era to uncover and
highlight the actual details of governance and corporate power that too often
remain unexplored. So sign up. You won't regret it.
